case: Three photos show a cart at 2 m, 3 m and 4 m, one second apart.
draw: Draw the three measured positions as blue dots on a number line. Label each with its time.
vary: If the pattern continues, where would the next dot go? Draw it with a dashed outline so a reader can tell it is a prediction.
frame: A measured position differs from a prediction because
example: A photo shows wet pavement.
nonexample: It must have rained.

case: A cart starts at 2 m, passes 6 m, and finishes at 4 m. Right is positive.
draw: Trace the two legs in pencil. Label the three positions in blue.
vary: On a second line draw one blue arrow from start to finish. Write the distance beside the path and the displacement beside the arrow.
frame: The path is longer than the displacement because
example: Walking from 1 m to 5 m changes your position.
nonexample: Adding every step tells you the change in position.

case: One cart goes from 8 m to 2 m in 3 s. Another goes from 2 m to 8 m in 3 s.
draw: Sketch both position–time lines on the same axes. Label t (s) and x (m).
vary: Draw a purple velocity arrow for each cart. Use the two slopes to decide what is equal and what has opposite signs.
frame: Both carts have the same speed, but
example: A cart moves at 2 m/s to the left.
nonexample: The cart’s speed is 2 m/s, with no direction given.

case: A cart moves at +2 m/s for 3 s and then at −2 m/s for 1 s.
draw: Draw both intervals on a velocity–time graph. Hatch the area below zero differently.
vary: Label the displacement for each interval, including its sign. Draw one blue arrow showing the combined displacement.
frame: The area below zero counts as
example: An area below the time axis represents negative displacement.
nonexample: Adding the magnitudes of both areas gives displacement in every trip.

case: A cart starts at 2 m. Its steady velocity could be anywhere from +2 to +3 m/s for the next 2 s.
draw: Mark the start, then draw one blue position dot for each possible endpoint at the two speed limits.
vary: Shade the interval between the dots. Label one finish inside the range and one outside.
frame: My endpoints change if
example: A forecast gives a lower and an upper endpoint.
nonexample: The cart will certainly stop at the midpoint.

case: Walk 3 m east, then 4 m north. One arrow can show your change in position.
draw: On a grid draw both legs tip-to-tail. Give every square the same scale.
vary: Draw the blue start-to-finish arrow. Compare its length with the total distance walked.
frame: The single arrow represents
example: A diagonal arrow connects the start of a trip to its finish.
nonexample: Two legs are listed separately without being combined.

case: At 0, 1 and 2 seconds, a bike is moving right at 6, 4 and 2 m/s.
draw: Draw three purple velocity arrows to scale. Label each speed and time.
vary: Draw the change in velocity between two arrows. Show how the bike can still move right as it slows down.
frame: The velocity points ___ while the change points
example: A bike turning at a steady speed changes its velocity.
nonexample: A bike moving straight at an unchanging speed has acceleration.

case: A car starts from rest and gains 3 m/s each second on a straight road.
draw: Draw purple velocity arrows at t = 0, 1 and 2 s; label the zero velocity without giving it a length.
vary: Sketch blue position dots for those times. Explain why equal changes in velocity do not give equal distances in equal times.
frame: The arrows change by ___ each second, while the gaps
example: A car gains 3 m/s in each successive second.
nonexample: A car moves at +3 m/s the entire time and therefore gains 3 m/s each second.

case: A puck glides right on nearly frictionless ice after the hand releases it.
draw: Sketch the released puck at three equal time intervals. Draw purple velocity arrows for zero net force.
vary: Now a brief leftward push acts. Draw a second sequence that shows what changes during that push. Label the force in orange.
frame: After release the puck keeps moving because
example: A released cart keeps its velocity when the net force is zero.
nonexample: Inertia is an extra forward push acting on the cart.

case: The same backpack is carried from Earth to the Moon. The Moon’s gravitational field is weaker.
draw: Draw the backpack twice. Give both drawings the same mass label in kilograms.
vary: Add orange weight arrows with different lengths. Label their unit and name which measurement changed.
frame: The mass stays ___, but the weight
example: Weight is the gravitational force on a backpack.
nonexample: A backpack’s mass in kilograms is its weight in newtons.

case: Two carts with masses 1 kg and 2 kg each experience the same 4 N net force.
draw: Draw both carts with equal orange net-force arrows. Label the variable you changed and the quantity you kept fixed.
vary: Draw how their purple velocities change after one second from rest. Explain which comparison tests the effect of mass.
frame: I can compare the two accelerations because
example: Two trials differ in mass while net force stays fixed.
nonexample: A second trial changes both the net force and the mass.

case: A 2 kg cart experiences net forces of 2 N, 4 N and 6 N in three trials.
draw: Sketch the trials with orange arrows to scale. Label what stays fixed.
vary: Plot the three force–acceleration points. Name both axes and use the origin to show what doubling the net force does.
frame: When net force doubles at fixed mass, acceleration
example: At fixed mass, twice the net force gives twice the acceleration.
nonexample: Any two quantities that both increase must be directly proportional.

case: A 2 kg cart feels 6 N right and 2 N left.
draw: Sketch both orange force arrows to scale on the same cart.
vary: Draw the single equivalent net-force arrow in a separate box. Add the acceleration magnitude and direction.
frame: I subtract these force magnitudes because
example: Two opposite pushes on one cart combine to a net force.
nonexample: A push on the cart and its reaction on a hand cancel on the cart.

case: A skater pushes a wall. The wall pushes the skater.
draw: Sketch the two objects and put one orange force arrow on each receiver. Name the source of each force.
vary: Redraw the skater alone. Include only the horizontal force acting on the skater. Explain why the pair does not cancel here.
frame: The partner force acts on
example: The wall pushes the hand and the hand pushes the wall.
nonexample: Weight and the normal force on a resting book form a third-law pair.

case: A lamp hangs motionless from one vertical rope.
draw: Circle the lamp as your chosen object. Name the two objects that exert forces on it.
vary: Replace the lamp with a dot. Draw orange arrows for each force, with labels and lengths consistent with the motion.
frame: I included ___ because it acts on
example: A diagram shows only forces acting on the selected lamp.
nonexample: A diagram puts the lamp’s pull on the ceiling on the lamp.

case: A crate rests on a ramp. Choose axes parallel and perpendicular to its surface.
draw: Draw the weight straight down in orange, then add both ramp axes in pencil.
vary: On a separate sketch resolve weight along the two axes with dashed projections. Explain why those projections do not add two new forces.
frame: Tilting the axes changes ___ but not
example: Part of weight acts parallel to the ramp axis.
nonexample: The two weight components are new forces in addition to weight.

case: A box remains at rest as a horizontal push increases from 2 N to 4 N. Both pushes are below the sliding threshold.
draw: Draw an orange push and friction arrow for each trial. Label both arrows in newtons.
vary: Draw a third moment just after sliding begins. Name the type of friction and explain what changed.
frame: Before sliding, friction changes to
example: Friction balances a gentle push while the surfaces do not slip.
nonexample: Static friction is always equal to its maximum.

case: A cart moves straight at +2 m/s while equal and opposite horizontal forces act.
draw: Sketch its orange forces. Draw its blue position dots one second apart.
vary: Show a second cart at rest with the same net force. Compare its position dots with those of the moving cart.
frame: Both carts are in equilibrium because
example: A cart moves straight at constant velocity with zero net force.
nonexample: An object that is momentarily at rest must be in equilibrium.

case: A student walks 4 m right and 4 m left, then writes “my displacement is 8 m.”
draw: Draw the route in pencil and mark the start and finish in blue. Circle the first mistaken claim.
vary: Show the distance and displacement separately, with units. Use the diagram to explain one correction.
frame: The 8 m measures ___; the endpoints show
example: Returning to the starting point gives zero displacement.
nonexample: A total of 8 m walked guarantees 8 m of displacement.

case: A 2 kg cart starts from rest with a constant 4 N net force right for 2 s.
draw: Draw and label the orange net force. Sketch how the purple velocity arrow changes each second.
vary: Use your arrows to sketch position dots at equal times. Explain what the dots would do if the net force became zero at 2 s.
frame: The force changes ___, so the spacing
example: A constant net force changes a cart’s velocity.
nonexample: A force is always needed to maintain an existing velocity.

case: A team reports that fictional asteroid XJ is “400 km away.” They have not said away from what.
draw: Draw Earth, XJ and a blue position axis. Label the zero, the positive direction and units.
vary: Add a second measured position at a later time. Mark what was measured and which assumption a forecast would need.
frame: A second team can interpret my position because
example: A position is reported from a chosen zero along a named positive axis.
nonexample: “It moved forward” specifies a frame without naming a reference.

case: A team predicts a cart will finish at 6–8 m. The next measured position is 9 m.
draw: Draw the predicted range and measured dot on the same blue position axis.
vary: Label the discrepancy. Sketch one measurement you would check or collect before revising the model.
frame: I would revise ___ if the new evidence shows
example: A team checks new measurements and changes its model assumption.
nonexample: A team erases the point because it falls outside the forecast.
